issues.legal_issue: A Hindu father's power to alienate his sons' interests in joint family property for untainted antecedent debts passes to the insolvency receiver and can be exercised through a receiver's sale.
material_facts: A Hindu father governed by Mitakshara law mortgaged joint family property for debts treated as antecedent and not shown to have been contracted for illegal or immoral purposes.
After the father was adjudged insolvent, the receiver sold the mortgaged property to a purchaser.
The sale occurred before the 1948 amendment that expressly made the relevant statutory provision retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The father's power to alienate his sons' interests passed to the receiver, and those interests vested in the purchaser at the receiver's sale; the sons could not independently redeem the property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28A of the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, as amended in 1948, provides retrospectively that an insolvent's property includes the capacity to exercise powers over property for the insolvent's benefit. The Court applied this to the father's power under Mitakshara law to alienate his sons' interests for untainted antecedent debts. It noted the earlier decision under the Presidency Towns Insolvency Act in Sat Narain v. Sri Kishen (63 I.A. 384), and the differing views under the Provincial Insolvency Act in Rama Sastrulu v. Balakrishna Rao (I.L.R. [1943] Mad. 83) and Viswanath v. Official Receiver (I.L.R. (1936) 16 Pat. 60).

issues.definition: When an insolvency receiver sells joint family property in a proceeding involving an insolvent Hindu father who could alienate his sons' interests for untainted antecedent debts, the purchaser acquires those interests.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser of an equity of redemption after a statutory debt-relief law begins may claim its benefits if the underlying debt existed and was payable by an agriculturist when the law began, and the purchaser meets the applicable qualification when applying.
material_facts: A purchaser acquired the equity of redemption after the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act had come into force and sought relief under that Act in a mortgage enforcement suit.
The mortgage debt existed before the Act came into force.
No question had been raised, and no evidence had been given, to establish that the original mortgagors were agriculturists or that the debt was payable by an agriculturist when the Act began.

The High Court had held that the purchaser was not an agriculturist, but the Supreme Court found it unnecessary to decide the disputed question concerning that status because the required fact about the debt had not been established.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to relief under the Act in this case because it was not established that the debt was payable by an agriculturist when the Act came into force. A purchaser's later acquisition of the equity of redemption does not itself prevent a claim if the statutory conditions are met.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 8(1) of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938, provide relief for qualifying debts payable by an agriculturist when the Act commenced. The right to seek relief is not confined to the original debtor and may be available to legal representatives and assigns; a purchaser's liability to pay a mortgage debt may arise on purchase even though the debt itself existed earlier. The purchaser must be an agriculturist when applying, and the debt must have been payable by an agriculturist when the Act commenced. The Court referred to Periannia v. Sellappa (I.L.R. [1939] Mad. 218).

predicates.mortgage_relief_claim_case: A purchaser seeks statutory debt relief in a mortgage enforcement proceeding.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_equity_after_relief_l: The purchaser acquired the equity of redemption after the relief law began.
predicates.debt_existed_when_relief_law_began: The underlying mortgage debt existed when the relief law began.

issues.definition: In a mortgage relief claim, a purchaser who acquired the equity after the relief law began is denied relief when the debt existed at that time but there is no proof it was then payable by an agriculturist.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgage stipulation for enhanced compound interest on default that is found to be penal does not justify awarding compound interest when the agreed ordinary rate was simple interest.
material_facts: The mortgage provided for simple interest at the ordinary rate and enhanced compound interest on default.
Both courts below found the default stipulation penal.
The High Court nevertheless awarded compound interest, having proceeded on the mistaken understanding that the original interest rate was compound.
issues.conclusion: The mortgage debt was to carry simple interest at the agreed ordinary rate until the end of the redemption period.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the finding that the enhanced compound-interest provision on default was a penalty, the Court held that compound interest should not have been allowed; the mortgage terms provided for simple interest at the ordinary rate. The trial court had referred to section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, but the Supreme Court's disposition rested on the penalty finding and the actual terms of the mortgage.

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_case: The proceeding seeks enforcement of a mortgage.
predicates.default_interest_stipulation_found_penal: The default stipulation for enhanced interest was found to be a penalty.
predicates.original_interest_rate_was_simple: The agreed ordinary rate of interest was simple interest.

issues.definition: In a mortgage enforcement proceeding, where the enhanced default-interest stipulation is penal and the agreed ordinary interest was simple, the debt carries simple interest until redemption.
